title: Half your skills came from work. Policy hasn't caught up
gist: Roughly half of a person's human capital is built at work rather than in school, yet around 70% of workers in low- and middle-income countries are in low-learning jobs — small-scale agriculture, low-quality self-employment or micro firms — versus 20% in high-income countries, and returns to experience for the self-employed are only half those of wage workers, leaving most of the learning potential of work untapped.

themes.theme: Half of human capital is built on the job

insights.claim: A global analysis of labor force surveys finds that work experience and education contribute roughly equally to the skills people carry through life, meaning about half of human capital is accumulated at work rather than in school.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: If half of skill formation happens in firms, the productivity policy lever sits with employers and firm quality, not only with school systems.
insights.quote: Roughly half of your human capital was probably gained on the job.
insights.locator: Where did you accumulate most of your human capital?

insights.claim: The estimate assumes a child completing 12 years of average-quality schooling — where a year of school returns 8 percent at average quality, with a harmonized learning outcome of 415 out of 615 — and 40 years in an average-quality job returning 2.5 percent a year at the average job mix of 55 percent wage employment.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The arithmetic is sensitive to the job-mix assumption, so economies with less wage employment get far less of the workplace learning dividend.
insights.locator: Note: Value refer to earnings gain from school and work

insights.claim: Workplace skill development remains largely absent from the human capital policy agenda, so factories, offices and farms get inadequate attention as settings where human capital is built.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A named policy blind spot: watch for on-the-job learning entering national human capital and jobs strategies, and the programs and providers that would fund.
insights.quote: A job is not just an income. It is a learning environment.
insights.locator: A job is not just an income

themes.theme: Most jobs in poor countries teach nothing

insights.claim: About 70 percent of workers in low- and middle-income countries work in small-scale agriculture, low-quality self-employment, or micro firms with fewer than five workers, compared with only 20 percent in high-income countries.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The employment composition gap — not just the schooling gap — mechanically caps skill accumulation and convergence in poor economies.
insights.locator: About 70 percent of workers in low-and middle-income countries

insights.claim: These low-learning jobs typically involve limited technology adoption, weak management practices and little exposure to new ways of working.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Explains why technology diffusion and management upgrading are prerequisites, not complements, to workforce skill gains.
insights.locator: These low-learning jobs often involve limited technology adoption

insights.claim: For the same gain in experience, earnings rise only half as much among the self-employed as among wage employees, so where a worker works determines how much they learn.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Self-employment-heavy labor markets should be modeled with structurally flatter lifetime earnings paths, which weakens the informal-sector-as-entrepreneurship narrative.

insights.claim: Access to workplace learning is gated first by employment itself: around 50 percent of women in low- and middle-income countries are out of the labor force and around 20 percent of youth are neither studying nor working.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Half the potential adult workforce is excluded from the main channel of skill formation, compounding the human capital gap each year.
insights.locator: First, to build human capital at work, you need to be employed

insights.claim: In Togo, a personal initiative program teaching small business entrepreneurs proactive entrepreneurial thinking raised profits by 30 percent — three times the gains of traditional training — and the effect persisted even eight years later.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: One of the few business-training results with large, durable effects; mindset-focused curricula outperform conventional content.
insights.quote: led to a 30 percent increase in profits — an impact that was three times the gains of traditional training and that persisted even eight years later

insights.claim: In India, on-the-job soft-skills training for garment workers — communication, time management, problem solving, decision-making and teamwork — raised productivity among trained workers by more than 13 percent, with spillovers to untrained workers on the same production line.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Spillovers mean firm-level returns exceed the private return to the trained worker, which is the economic case for training subsidies.
insights.locator: In India, a workplace on-the-job training for garment workers

insights.claim: A review of evidence in six African countries shows that firms with better internet connectivity were not only more likely to provide on-the-job training but also exported and sold more.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Links digital infrastructure directly to firm-level training and export performance — a second-order argument for connectivity capex.
insights.locator: They can also support technology adoption

insights.claim: Job placement services and apprenticeship programs reviewed in Brazil, Colombia, Côte d'Ivoire and Uganda showed real gains in both skills and earnings, while childcare access significantly increases female labor force participation though service quality and cost remain critical constraints.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Concrete, evaluated entry points for getting more people into the learning environment of work.

themes.theme: The firm-skill virtuous cycle and how countries entered it

insights.claim: More productive firms create more learning opportunities and better-skilled workers make firms more productive and innovative, so the two reinforce each other and countries that break into this virtuous cycle pull ahead.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A self-reinforcing mechanism implies threshold dynamics and divergence between economies, not smooth convergence.
insights.quote: The two reinforce each other. Countries that break into this virtuous cycle can pull ahead.
insights.locator: More jobs with stronger learning potential

insights.claim: Bangladesh's garment industry was catalyzed when Multi-Fibre Arrangement export quotas on Korean producers pushed production to unconstrained Bangladesh and the firm Desh Garments partnered with Korea's Daewoo in 1979 to train 130 Bangladeshi workers and managers, whose skills spread as trainees founded or joined other firms.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A trade restriction plus one training partnership seeded a national export industry — a reminder that skill spillovers from FDI can dwarf the direct investment.

insights.claim: In China, growth in college-educated workers, particularly in science and engineering, boosted innovation, productivity and trade.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Supports the STEM-supply channel as a driver of trade competitiveness, relevant when assessing other countries' education expansions.
insights.locator: In China, growth in college-educated workers

insights.claim: In Costa Rica the government worked with firms and education partners to provide industry-specific training in high tech, and this co-investment helped establish high-tech operations and later retain higher-value R&D activities in the country.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Targeted skills co-investment is the mechanism by which an assembly location moves up to R&D — a template for nearshoring destinations.
insights.locator: In Costa Rica, the government worked with firms

insights.claim: Governments can lower the cost of workplace learning to firms through co-financing schemes, training subsidies and technical assistance, and by supporting technology adoption since digital tools reduce the cost of finding information, managing workflows and staying connected.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Names the fiscal instruments that would channel public money into firm-level training markets.
